title: Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation Modulated Thylakoid-Enzyme Interfacial Coupling for Enhanced Light-Powered Biocatalysis.
authors: Zhang, Jiayi; Ding, Chengtao; Zhang, Xiaoyan; Fan, Daidi; Liu, Jiaxu; Bai, Yunpeng
abstract: Thylakoid (TK) membranes serve as promising photosynthesis platforms for light-driven biocatalysis, yet their catalytic efficiency is largely restricted by poor coupling between photo-dependent NADPH regeneration and enzymatic conversion. Herein, we report a facile TK-anchored enzyme condensate strategy to overcome this bottleneck. Specifically, the UTX-derived intrinsically disordered region (IDR) fused with target enzymes mediates liquid-liquid phase separation to form enzyme-rich condensates, which then stably anchor on TK membranes and spatially confine catalysis at the NADPH-generating membrane interface. Taking carbonyl reductase SmCR(V4) and ene-reductase SsER(A314S) as model enzymes, the TK-enzyme hybrid condensates exhibit prominently improved catalytic performance, especially under NADPH regeneration-limited conditions, relative to freely dispersed enzyme systems. The TK-UTX-SmCR(V4) hybrid improves the total product yield up to 3.1-fold, and the TK-UTX-SsER(A314S) hybrid reaches a 2.9-fold higher conversion within 20 min. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations validate a dynamic multivalent interfacial anchoring mode: the IDR domain mediates stable membrane binding via high-frequency residue-lipid interactions dominated by short-range Lennard-Jones forces (with auxiliary electrostatic contributions), while the enzyme domain remains solvent-exposed. This work establishes a feasible strategy that physically links light-driven NADPH recycling with enzymatic catalysis, offering a general approach for constructing high-efficiency artificial photosynthesis systems.

title: Membrane orientation regulates GAPR-1 oligomerization that is suitable for interaction with beclin 1.
authors: Shen, Ziying; Corey, Robin A; van Doorne, Hidde; Verhoek, Iris; Koopman, Renee; Huitema, Daniel S; Sardana, Samiksha; Baggelaar, Marc P; Stansfeld, Phillip J; Kaloyanova, Dora V; Helms, J Bernd
journal: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS
abstract: Golgi-associated plant pathogenesis-related protein 1 (GAPR-1) is a beclin 1-interacting peripheral membrane protein that is anchored to the Golgi complex via an N-myristoyl-group and ionic interactions. Here we investigated the determinants of GAPR-1 membrane binding using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and applied the results to investigate the subsequent oligomerization into biomolecular condensates and interaction with beclin 1. MD simulations revealed a specific orientation of GAPR-1 upon docking to a negatively charged lipid bilayer involving lysines at position 7 and 33 (Lys7 and Lys33). Substitution of these lysines with glutamine changed the preferred membrane orientation of GAPR-1. Upon deletion of the myristoyl-group, GAPR-1 remained docked to the lipid bilayer, but lost its preferred orientation, suggesting that myristoylation constrained the dynamics of the protein at the membrane surface. Upon mutation of Lys7 to glutamine and expression in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, [K7Q]GAPR-1 was prevented from myristoylation and condensate formation was severely impaired. Similar results were obtained when N-terminal myristoylation of GAPR-1 was prevented by mutating amino acid Gly2. However, in contrast to [G2A]GAPR-1, [K7Q]GAPR-1 could not interact with beclin 1 anymore upon co-expression in yeast cells, and failed to interfere with beclin 1-dependent autophagy in human cells. Our combined data show that GAPR-1 requires a defined orientation at the membrane to control protein homo-and hetero-oligomerization and to execute its function. We revealed a novel function of protein myristoylation in which it determines the motional freedom of specific protein orientations, which may have relevance for the entire myristoylated proteome.

title: Integrative Structural Modeling of Intrinsically Disordered Regions in a Human HDAC2 Chromatin Remodeling Complex.
authors: Nde, Jules; Kempf, Cassandra G; Zimmermann, Rosalyn C; Cesare, Joseph; Zhang, Ying; Workman, Jerry L; Florens, Laurence; Washburn, Michael P
abstract: Histone deacetylase-containing complexes play central roles in chromatin regulation, yet the structural organization of their intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the previously uncharacterized protein C16orf87, which we renamed MHAP1, as a binding partner of HDAC2 and MIER1. Because all three proteins contain extensive IDRs that remain difficult to study using single structural analysis methods, we employed an integrative structural approach combining cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) with integrative structural modeling to define the architecture of the complex. The resulting integrative structural model reveals that the previously uncharacterized C-terminal IDR of HDAC2 acts as a key interaction hub, engaging both the ELM2 domain of MIER1 and the N- and C-terminal regions of MHAP1. These findings provide the first structural framework for the interactions among HDAC2:MIER1:MHAP1 and demonstrate how intrinsically disordered regions can mediate assembly of a chromatin-associated deacetylase complex. Finally, this research further demonstrates the ability of XL-MS to facilitate integrative structural modeling of protein complexes. Mass spectrometry data may be accessed through ProteomeXchange via PXD082280 and the MassIVE repository MSV000102752.

title: Quantitative Model of Transcriptional Noise Regulation by mRNA Condensates.
authors: Lanitis, Andreas; Kolomeisky, Anatoly B
journal: The journal of physical chemistry letters
abstract: A fundamental biological process of transcription occurs in the cell nucleus, which is a complex medium that also contains multiple heterogeneous structures known as biomolecular condensates. Interestingly, some of these condensates contain mRNA molecules in addition to proteins, suggesting an important cellular role in transcription that is not yet well understood. In this work, we develop a minimal theoretical framework for quantitative investigation of the role of reversible mRNA condensation in transcription. Our discrete-state stochastic approach accounts for the most relevant processes, allowing us to explicitly evaluate the properties of the system and clarify the effects of condensation. Analytical calculations supported by computer simulations suggest that reversible mRNA condensation influences the transcription processes by maintaining a constant level of free mRNA in the nucleoplasm while lowering the degree of stochastic noise and increasing the robustness against external perturbations. Physicochemical arguments are presented to explain these observations. The proposed theoretical framework elucidates important microscopic aspects of transcription, providing a convenient quantitative tool for investigating complex biological phenomena.

title: Convergence Mechanisms of Generative Models in Molecular Conformational Sampling.
authors: B E, Nagesh; Mondal, Jagannath
journal: Journal of chemical theory and computation
abstract: Characterizing equilibrium conformational ensembles with deep generative models requires understanding whether a model reproduces a target distribution and how it reaches that distribution. Here, we compare two generative routes to molecular conformational sampling, stochastic relaxation and deterministic transport, using denoising diffusion probabilistic models and rectified-flow models across systems of increasing complexity: a multimodal two-dimensional potential, the folded miniprotein Trp-cage, and a high-dimensional dihedral representation of an intrinsically disordered protein. We show that these paradigms differ in end point fidelity and in how distributional error is resolved during sampling. Diffusion models converge through pronounced late-stage stochastic relaxation and robustly recover the configurational breadth across neural architectures. Rectified flow approaches the target distribution through deterministic transport and therefore depends more strongly on architectural expressivity, particularly in heterogeneous, high-dimensional landscapes. Entropy and moment-evolution analyses further show that diffusion more reliably restores the ensemble location and fluctuation structure, whereas rectified flow requires Transformer-level feature mixing to represent transport geometry accurately. These results establish the convergence mechanism as a practical design principle for molecular generative sampling, clarifying when stochastic diffusion provides robustness and when deterministic transport requires higher representational capacity.

title: MOFF2: A Transferable Coarse-Grained Protein Force Field for Predictive Condensate Simulations.
authors: Liu, Shuming; Zhang, Yumeng; Riveros, Ivan; Wang, Cong; Zhang, Bin
journal: Journal of chemical theory and computation
abstract: Coarse-grained (CG) protein force fields enable simulations of biomolecular systems at length and time scales that are difficult to access with atomistic models, but achieving transferability across folded, intrinsically disordered, and multidomain proteins (MDPs) remains challenging. A central difficulty is that one-bead-per-residue models must represent chemically specific residue interactions while also absorbing solvent-mediated and many-body effects into a simplified energy function. Here, we present MOFF2, a transferable coarse-grained protein force field that combines residue-pair-specific interactions with a density-dependent many-body potential. MOFF2 is optimized using a two-stage strategy: bottom-up parameter learning from heterogeneous reference ensembles followed by refinement against experimental conformational observables. The resulting model provides balanced performance across ordered proteins (OPs), intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), and multidomain proteins, and predicts condensate saturation-concentration trends for A1-LCD variant systems. Analysis of the learned parameters reveals chemically interpretable interaction patterns and density-dependent effects that explain the model's improved transferability. These results demonstrate that combining a generalized coarse-grained energy function with data-driven optimization can produce a practical and interpretable force field for protein conformational and condensate simulations.

title: How a Highly Acidic SH3 Domain Binds to Its Intrinsically Disordered Partner through the Formation of an Encounter Complex Intermediate.
authors: Jaramillo-Martinez, Valeria; Kukreja, Ritika; Cohen, Michaela R; Mujica, Ally; Barton, Samuel; Onwuzulu, Oluebube C; Cardoso, Jorge; Dominguez, Matthew J; Kekwick, Isabelle M; Ali, Jaden; Bell, Gemma M; Rice, Sydney; Poaquiza, Daniela; McClure, Colin; Anguiano, Frida; Latham, Michael P; Ball, K Aurelia; Stollar, Elliott J
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: Electrostatic interactions often play a role in determining the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of protein-protein interactions. However, the role of long-range electrostatic interactions in intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) binding is less clear, as they often bind in multiple steps, including initial formation of a disordered encounter complex, followed by rearrangement into the bound state. We varied the salt concentration to probe the role of long-range electrostatic interactions in the binding of the highly charged AbpSH3 domain and the oppositely charged IDP ArkA. Using isothermal titration calorimetry, we observed that salt enthalpically destabilizes the bound complex. Molecular dynamics and NMR experiments revealed that salt has little effect on the bound state structure. However, simulations show that salt destabilizes the encounter complex intermediate, which primarily affects the association rate as measured by NMR. Consistent with these results, salt has the largest stabilizing effect on the apo SH3 domain, as cations substitute for the transient and long-range electrostatic interactions that can form with ArkA in the complex. We revealed a detailed picture of how a highly charged domain uses long-range, fuzzy, electrostatic interactions to help reach the bound state, a mechanism that is likely common among other highly charged domains that bind IDPs.

title: Origin of the Anomalous Guest Polymer Selectivity in Complex Coacervates.
authors: Wu, Zongpei; Sabadini, Julia Bonesso; Walker, Pierre J; Loh, Watson; Wang, Zhen-Gang; Perry, Sarah L; Chen, Shensheng
abstract: Complex coacervates horizontal line liquid condensates resulting from liquid-liquid phase separation of oppositely charged polymers horizontal line have attracted broad interest in artificial cells, drug delivery vehicles, and smart nanoreactors. The functionality of these applications is significantly influenced by the coacervate's ability to encapsulate guest macromolecules, where the guest interactions determine their loading efficiency and activity. Using MD simulations, analytical theory, and experiments, we demonstrate that the intrinsic electrostatic correlations within the coacervate matrix significantly modify the effective interactions of guest polymers in the dense phase, resulting in the strong dependence of encapsulation on guest chain length, charge density, and charge sequence observed experimentally. Even in the absence of chemical incompatibility, neutral polymers are strongly excluded from the coacervate phase as a result of disrupting electrostatic correlations within coacervates. Consequently, the encapsulation efficiency of neutral polymers exponentially decays with increasing guest chain length. For polyampholyte-like intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), their effective interaction within coacervates is largely determined by charge sequence: IDPs with more-disordered sequences experience strict rejection from the dense phase, whereas those with more blocky charges are dispersed within coacervates. Interestingly, for all the guest species tested, their effective interactions are opposite to those observed in dilute solutions, where the sign of the effective two-body interaction reverses when going from the dilute phase to the dense coacervate phase. We elucidate that the non-trivial guest selectivity in complex coacervates originates from the disruption of polycation-polyanion electrostatic correlations by the guest, which combines an energetic penalty (dilution of charge density) with an entropic penalty (loss of chain conformational freedom of the host). These findings have significant implications for understanding guest behavior in coacervate and biocondensate systems.

title: Conformational Landscape of a Marginally Disordered Protein HYPK and its Charge-Variant Mutant in the Context of Folded Domains.
authors: Gaalswyk, Kari; Gruebele, Martin; Ghosh, Kingshuk
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) can have varying proportions of disordered and structured regions, and various fractions of amino acids promoting these regions. This raises the possibility that some IDPs may behave as marginal proteins, exhibiting properties of both disordered and folded states. HYPK is one such recently discovered marginal protein studied by fluorescence assays (with fluorescent proteins attached at the termini) and circular dichroism (CD) while modulating temperature, crowding, ionic strength and sequence (by altering charge composition and patterning). Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to understand the sequence-specific and structural origin of this marginality by investigating the conformation landscape of both the wild-type and a charge-variant mutant of HYPK, with and without fluorescent proteins (FPs) attached at the N- and C- termini. We find the charge-variant mutant is more compact compared to the wild type both with and without FPs, showing the importance of charge patterning that is consistent with experimental observations and theoretical predictions used for experimental characterization. The wild-type HYPK fused to FPs reveals two distinct conformational populations differing in helix packing, which may account for the marginality observed experimentally. The charge-variant mutant protein with FPs also displays bimodal conformational populations, but through a different mechanism involving competitive electrostatic interactions between different protein segments and the FPs. Bimodality is observed in the mutant without FPs under different salt conditions due to competitive interactions between different segments of the chain or between the chain and counterions, while it becomes less evident in the wild-type HYPK without the crowding and surface interactions provided by the FPs. These findings offer broad insights into the origin of marginality, competing interactions, as well as the roles charge patterning and folded domains play on IDP conformation both in vitro and in-cell.

title: Structure-Guided Terminal Modifications Enhance the Efficiency of PET Degradation.
authors: Zhang, Lin; Chen, Keyan; Xi, Zhiwen; Tian, Zhuo; Wei, Xuyang; Aqma, Wan Syaidatul; Guo, Zhiguo; Wang, Qi; Niu, Qiuhong
abstract: Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is a widely used plastic whose persistence and improper disposal pose serious environmental and health risks. In this study, three novel PET hydrolases TbPETase, AbPETase, and AfPETase were identified from Thermoanaerobacterales, Acidimicrobiales, and Actinokineospora fastidiosa, respectively. Among these, TbPETase exhibited the highest enzymatic activity and thermostability. Based on structural analysis, we performed semirational truncations targeting the intrinsically disordered N- and C-terminal regions of TbPETase, generating two improved variants DeltaN36 and DeltaC4. The double mutant, TbPETaseDeltaN36/DeltaC4, demonstrated a 2.3-fold increase in overall enzymatic activity and a 2.6-fold improvement in catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) compared to the wild-type enzyme, along with significantly enhanced thermal stability. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the removal of flexible terminal regions increased the overall structural rigidity of TbPETaseDeltaN36/DeltaC4. This structural stabilization was associated with the formation of a hydrogen bond at T215 and a pi-pi stacking interaction at W193. In a 100 mL one-pot reaction system, the combination of TbPETaseDeltaN36/DeltaC4 with an engineered BMHETase variant, BMHETase6M, achieved 81.2% degradation of semicrystalline PET powder at 60  degrees C over 60 h, yielding terephthalic acid as the major product. These findings demonstrate the potential of TbPETaseDeltaN36/DeltaC4 as a highly efficient and industrially applicable biocatalyst for PET degradation.

title: Revealing protein structural transitions in the era of generative artificial intelligence.
authors: Hung, Ta I; Venkatesan, Raghu; Chang, Chia-En A
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and deep generative models have greatly accelerated the generation of protein conformational ensembles. Moving beyond isolated structural states to reconstruct continuous, physically realistic transition pathways further provides mechanistic understanding to guide molecular design but remains a significant challenge. This review examines emerging computational approaches for modeling protein conformational transitions, from classical molecular dynamics simulations to deep learning-based latent space interpolation. Recent developments in capturing natural molecular motions are discussed, particularly via internal coordinate representations and physics-informed models. We also examine the complexity of modeling highly dynamic systems, such as intrinsically disordered proteins, and the role of the cellular environment. Integrating experimental data with simulated structural ensembles represents a promising direction for future methodologies. Nonetheless, key challenges remain, including maintaining physical realism throughout transition trajectories, capturing environment-dependent energy landscapes, and predicting dynamically consistent pathways with accurate transition kinetics.

title: Binding without Docking: Small-Molecule Binding Paths on Disordered Proteins.
authors: Louet, Adelie; Hummer, Gerhard; Vendruscolo, Michele
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Disordered proteins are challenging targets for drug design because they lack well-defined binding pockets. Small molecules can bind them, but when the bound state remains conformationally heterogeneous, these interactions are not readily characterized in terms of conventional binding pockets. Here, we use the concept of binding paths to describe how small molecules interact with disordered proteins. A binding path is a stochastic sequence of transient residue clusters that a ligand engages as it diffuses across a disordered protein, with each cluster forming and breaking up on time scales comparable to the overall residence time. We formalize this approach using a Markov state model (MSM), in which each state corresponds to a set of residues simultaneously contacting the ligand and the transition probabilities capture how the ligand moves between these sets. We apply this framework to the interactions of 10074-G5 with Abeta42 and of fasudil with alpha-synuclein, two disordered proteins associated with Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, respectively. The MSM enables both a dynamic mapping of transient binding sites and a calculation of dissociation constants consistent with experimental measurements. By generalizing the concept of static binding pockets to dynamic binding paths, this approach provides a quantitative framework for characterizing small-molecule binding by disordered proteins and for identifying druggable regions on these challenging targets.

title: Capillary physics links HIV capsid geometry to nuclear pore translocation.
authors: Brown, Alexander W; Al-Izzi, Sami C; Parker, Jack L; Hertel, Sophie; Jacques, David A; Kusumaatmaja, Halim; Morris, Richard G
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: The protective capsid encasing the genetic material of HIV can traverse the nuclear pore complex (NPC) intact, despite being far larger than conventional passive cargo. This is attributed to the properties of the capsid surface, which promote partitioning into cohesive assemblies of the disordered proteins that form the NPC's permeability barrier: phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins (FG-Nups). The implication, at the mesoscale, is that capsid-NPC interactions are characterized by the interfacial physics of wetting and capillarity. To capture this, we develop a minimal theory that reduces to an interplay between capsid geometry, effective cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic contact angles, and a ratio of interfacial tensions. By combining analytical calculations, sharp- and diffuse-interface numerics, we make several predictions: A geometry-dependent trade-off between penetration depth and the wetting transition; asymmetric capillary forces that generate torques and lead to metastable "stalled" states that are tilted; a topological classification of the possible mechanisms underlying the largest energetic barrier; and spontaneous symmetry breaking of displaced FG-Nups. These behaviors connect capsid shape and orientation to the topology and symmetry of FG-Nup displacement, and to the molecular compositions on each side of the pore. They are consistent with published cryoelectron tomography orientations, which provide an initial estimate of the cytoplasmic contact angle. Crucially, our results identify a capillary advantage for the HIV capsid's characteristic broken-symmetry geometry.

title: Exploring the Mutual Effects of Excipients and Proteins in Complex Coacervation.
authors: Zeng, Xianci; Sathyavageeswaran, Arvind; Zajac, Jonathan W P; Heldt, Caryn L; Sarupria, Sapna; Perry, Sarah L
abstract: Complex coacervation is a type of associative liquid-liquid phase separation driven by the electrostatic complexation of oppositely-charged macromolecules. Coacervate materials have shown significant potential for the formulation of proteins and viruses with improved thermal stability. We leveraged a combination of experiments and simulations to investigate how the presence of both proteins and small-molecule excipients common in stabilizing formulations would affect the partitioning of both protein and excipient in the coacervate phase. Although electrostatic interactions tend to dominate the incorporation of proteins into coacervates, our study highlights the balance of protein-water-excipient interactions as a critical parameter for understanding partitioning trends in these multi-component formulations. This work provides insight into the design of multi-component formulations that take advantage of complex coacervation and could serve as a basis for product design in the future.

title: The AML-Associated A338V Mutation Rewires GPR183 Signaling through C-Terminal Ensemble Redistribution.
authors: Andersson, Louise; Wesolowski, Patryk A; Jahrstorfer, Laura; Rosa, Alexander De; Heger, Tomas; Neuman, Vilmos; Sieradzan, Adam K; Wales, David J; Kozielewicz, Pawel
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) rely on dynamic conformational ensembles to coordinate G protein activation and recruitment of regulatory transducers such as GPCR kinases and beta-arrestins. The oxysterol receptor GPR183 has been implicated in hematological malignancies, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where a rare A338V substitution occurs within its intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail. Here, we combined bioluminescence/fluorescence resonance energy transfer, bioluminescence- and fluorescence-based assays as well as migration experiments, with molecular dynamics simulations and allosteric communication networks to define the structural and functional consequences of this mutation. The A338V variant preserved agonist potency and largely maintained or even enhanced agonist-induced Gi protein activation, likely by inducing different receptor core conformations. On the other hand, it consistently impaired GRK2 and beta-arrestin2 recruitment across multiple experimental configurations. Atomistic simulations supported these observations and further suggested that A338V reshapes the conformational ensemble of the C-terminal tail, altering its disorder, compaction, and membrane interactions. In particular, the mutation redistributes lipid interactions of phosphorylation-prone serine and threonine residues within the tail, suggesting disrupted spatial presentation of regulatory motifs required for productive GRK2 and beta-arrestin coupling. Importantly, overexpression of GPR183 A338V in differentiated HL-60 cells led to a significant increase in migration of these cells toward the chemoattractant. Together, these results identify the intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail of GPR183 as a determinant of selective transducer coupling and show how a single naturally occurring mutation within a GPCR intrinsically disordered region can alter its conformational ensemble, selectively modulate intracellular protein coupling, and affect receptor-mediated cellular behavior.

title: Random Hybrid Polypeptides Regulate Immune Signaling through Promiscuous and Dynamic Interaction Landscapes.
authors: Chen, Haolin; Zhou, Haisen; Jin, Tianyi; Zhang, Zhihui; Zhao, Zhenzhong; Cai, Haoran; Yu, Xiaoman; Liu, Hong; Chen, Shi; Li, Chuang; Yan, Xuehai; Wu, Guangqi; Qi, Miao; Liu, Lixin; Chen, Yongming; Lu, Hua
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: We developed a high-throughput synthesis and screening workflow combined with machine-learning-assisted optimization to identify functional compositions for immunomodulation in random hybrid polypeptides (RHPs). Using a selenium-containing polypeptide platform, we constructed a nucleoside-functionalized RHP library incorporating nucleoside, cationic, and anionic interaction motifs. Machine-learning-assisted optimization of this library identified a lead RHP, termed IDP-IMP (intrinsically disordered protein-inspired immunomodulatory polypeptide), that suppresses CpG DNA-Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) signaling with limited cytotoxicity. Rather than acting as a conventional strong nucleic acid scavenger or TLR9 antagonist, IDP-IMP showed moderate binding/association with both CpG and TLR9 through different side chain compositions, leading to reduced intracellular CpG-TLR9 colocalization. Across the polymer library, stronger CpG binding did not necessarily correspond to greater inhibitory activity, indicating that CpG binding alone did not predict functional activity. In a collagen-induced arthritis rat model, IDP-IMP attenuated inflammation and joint pathology without detectable systemic toxicity. These findings demonstrate a high-throughput approach for identifying statistical polymer compositions perturbing CpG-TLR9 signaling. The results highlight the importance of IDP-like weak, multivalent, and dynamic interactions in immunomodulation.

title: Impairing Golgin-45 transcription factor activity unleashes malignant secretion in lung cancer.
authors: Wu, Chao; Kumar, Abhishek; Wang, Shike; Zhao, Weina; Xi, Yuanxin; Wang, Jing; Jain, Abhinav K; Russell, William K; Guo, Hou-Fu; Tan, Xiaochao; Kurie, Jonathan M
abstract: Golgin-45 (G45) is a coiled-coil protein that transits reversibly between the Golgi and nucleus. In the Golgi, G45 serves as a tether for effectors of a pro-tumorigenic secretory program, but its nuclear role remains unclear. Here, we report that, upon entering the nucleus, G45 functions as a basic leucine zipper transcription factor. From genomic mapping, RNA-sequencing, and functional validation studies, we identify G45-binding sites and show that nuclear G45 can function as a transcriptional activator or repressor, a versatility enabled by phase separation into nuclear bodies enriched in transcriptional co-regulators. In lung cancer models, Golgi-docking reinforces, whereas nuclear translocation opposes, pro-tumorigenic activity of G45. Nuclear G45 incorporates into dimeric transcription factors that silence pro-tumorigenic secreted cargos. Epigenetic events in lung cancer degrade nuclear G45 and sequester G45 in the Golgi, which unleashes malignant secretion. Thus, inter-organelle transitions govern a G45-dependent secretory axis that drives lung cancer progression.

title: Nodule Cysteine-Rich (NCR) Peptides as Next-Generation Antimicrobials: A Computational Perspective on Structure, Mechanism, and Drug Design.
authors: Pawar, Yash; Bidvi, Sneha; Choure, Rajendra
abstract: The rapid escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has rendered conventional antibiotics increasingly ineffective, necessitating the exploration of alternative therapeutic strategies. Nodule-specific cysteine-rich (NCR) peptides, a diverse class of plant-derived antimicrobial peptides produced by legumes, have emerged as promising candidates due to their potent and multifaceted biological activity. Unlike traditional antibiotics that target a single cellular pathway, NCR peptides exhibit pleiotropic mechanisms, including membrane disruption, transporter-mediated internalization, intracellular targeting of essential regulatory proteins, and metabolic interference. Recent advances have revealed that their activity is governed not only by primary sequence but also by complex structural determinants such as disulfide bond topology and intrinsically disordered functional domains. Furthermore, their broad-spectrum efficacy, including activity against biofilms and cross-kingdom pathogens, highlights their therapeutic potential in combating multidrug-resistant infections. Computational approaches - molecular dynamics simulations, flexible docking algorithms, and artificial intelligence-based design frameworks - are increasingly proposed as a route to optimizing peptide structure, stability, and target specificity. These individual tools have each been validated in other peptide contexts and, in a small number of cases, directly on NCR peptides; their assembly into a single, discovery-to-validation pipeline for NCR engineering, however, is a synthesis proposed by this review rather than a workflow that has itself been experimentally validated end-to-end. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the structural features, multimodal mechanisms, and computational strategies associated with NCR peptides, explicitly distinguishing experimentally established findings from the proposed in silico pipeline and its current, largely untested assumptions. It also examines current challenges, including instability, unpredictable toxicity, assay-dependent variability, and the still-preliminary evidence for reduced resistance development, and outlines a moderated set of future directions for AI-driven peptide engineering. On present, largely preclinical evidence, NCR peptides represent a promising - but not yet clinically validated - platform warranting further mechanistic and computational investigation as part of the broader antimicrobial pipeline.

title: Determinants of centromeric nucleosome conformation.
authors: Paintsil, Emeleeta A; Lee, Joshua; Meidl Zahorodny, Sarah S; Wereszczynski, Jeff; Morrison, Emma A
abstract: Centromeric chromatin is defined by the presence of the histone H3 variant CENP-A, which forms a specialized nucleosome required for kinetochore assembly. Compared to canonical H3 nucleosomes, CENP-A nucleosomes exhibit an open DNA conformation that leaves an additional 13 base pairs of DNA accessible at the entry and exit sites. While the CENP-A alphaN-helix has previously been implicated in promoting this enhanced DNA breathing, the contributions of the intrinsically disordered N-terminal tail and adjacent latch regions of CENP-A to nucleosome conformation remain unknown. The intrinsically disordered N-terminal regions of histone H3 are known to facilitate interactions with DNA to stabilize overall nucleosome conformation. Here, we utilized a combination of MNase digestion assays and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of nucleosomes containing targeted swaps of the H3 and CENP-A tail, latch, and alphaN-helix regions to systematically test the contribution of each N-terminal histone region to nucleosomal DNA conformation. Substitution of individual H3 N-terminal regions with those of CENP-A opened the DNA at the entry/exit sites and increased DNA accessibility. While any single CENP-A N-terminal region was sufficient to open the canonical nucleosomal DNA conformation, replacement of any single CENP-A N-terminal region with its H3 counterpart was insufficient to restore the closed DNA conformation characteristic of canonical H3 nucleosomes. Instead, progressive incorporation of multiple H3-derived regions produced increasingly closed DNA conformations, demonstrating that the H3 tail, latch, and alphaN-helices act cooperatively to stabilize wrapped nucleosomal DNA. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the more restricted DNA breathing of canonical nucleosomes arises from coordinated contributions across multiple N-terminal regions and suggest that the multi-region redundancy in the conformational flexibility of the centromeric nucleosome could emphasize the importance of retaining flexibility in the centromeric nucleosome, even upon post-translational modification and binding to structural proteins.

title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models.
authors: Cullen, Mina; Biancaniello, Carmen; Taskova, Katerina; Miletic, Vedran; De Simone, Alfonso; Mercadante, Davide
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from C(alpha)-only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to explore phenomena such as secondary structure propensity and nucleation in condensates, conformationally selected binding motifs across disordered ensembles or conformational preferences of sequence-specific short-linear motifs.

title: Complex post-traumatic stress disorder in refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced people: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Melkam, Mamaru; Xu, Cheng; Maccallum, Fiona; Oestreich, Lena
abstract: Background: Forcibly displaced populations, including refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced persons, are frequently exposed to severe, prolonged and repeated trauma from which escape is difficult or impossible. Such exposures increase the risk for complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD), defined by core PTSD symptoms alongside disturbances in self-organisation (DSO), including affective dysregulation, negative self-concept, and relational difficulties. However, the prevalence of CPTSD in forcibly displaced populations has not yet been quantitatively synthesised, and the added value of the CPTSD construct over PTSD in this population has not been examined.Methods: This systematic review and meta-analysis searched five databases from inception to January 2026. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to estimate pooled CPTSD prevalence, with pre-specified subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses.Results: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria, representing 17 independent samples (n = 12,504). Reported CPTSD prevalence varied from 3.0% to 74.6%. The random-effects pooled prevalence, retained as a descriptive summary of the included studies, was 20.9% (95% CI [12.6%, 32.6%]), the 95% prediction interval was [1.7%, 80.3%]. Between-study heterogeneity was very high (I(2) = 98.3%). Recruitment context was strongly associated with prevalence: estimates averaged 10.6% in community-based samples and 55.2% in treatment-seeking samples. Asylum seekers exhibited markedly higher prevalence than refugees. Across four studies, post-migration living difficulties, including legal insecurity, poverty, and marginalisation, were more strongly associated with DSO symptoms than with core PTSD symptoms, suggesting that ongoing structural adversity actively perpetuates complex trauma psychopathology beyond pre-migration trauma alone.Conclusion: Available evidence indicates marked variation in CPTSD prevalence across forcibly displaced populations rather than a single generalisable prevalence rate. Recruitment context accounts for part of this variation, but the limited and geographically uneven evidence base prevents global population-level inference. Future studies should use representative sampling and consistently report displacement, trauma, and post-migration characteristics to permit more informative explanations of between-population variation.

title: GeoSeq-EGNN: A geometry-sequence fused equivariant graph neural network for predicting short linear motifs within intrinsically disordered regions.
authors: Zhang, Jun; Zhang, Jinming; Zheng, Liting; Ruan, Huiqiong; Li, Yuxiang; Li, Yi; Luo, Guilan
abstract: Short linear motifs (SLiMs) located within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are essential for mediating dynamic protein-protein interactions. However, their short length, sequence degeneracy, and the conformational heterogeneity of IDRs pose significant challenges for accurate computational identification. Traditional methods that rely exclusively on one-dimensional sequences or static three-dimensional structures may not adequately capture the intricate interplay between structure and sequence, while severe class imbalance often results in unacceptably high false-positive rates. To address these challenges, we introduce GeoSeq-EGNN, a Geometry-Sequence Fused Equivariant Graph Neural Network designed for dual-modality SLiMs prediction. This architecture effectively integrates Global-Local Hybrid Equivariant Message Passing Layers (GLH-EMPL) to model the three-dimensional spatial folding dynamics of IDRs, alongside Multi-Scale Geometry-Sequence Fusion Network Layers (MSGS-FNL) that utilize Bidirectional LSTMs to extract critical one-dimensional primary sequence topologies. We also incorporate an adaptive coordinate update mechanism to improve geometric stability in deeper layers and dynamic gate feature fusion to reduce representation over-smoothing. To address class imbalance, we use a confidence-aware focal loss that penalizes overconfident erroneous predictions. On the evaluated SLiMs dataset, GeoSeq-EGNN achieved an accuracy of 92.94% and an AUPRC of 82.17% under the final F6 feature configuration and outperformed the evaluated baseline models in the controlled one-hot comparison, with higher Precision and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). These results support GeoSeq-EGNN as a computational framework for SLiM prediction and provide a basis for future studies of SLiM-mediated regulatory networks.

title: An intrinsically disordered adaptor protein controls the size and composition of EGFR condensates on membranes
authors: Maria F. Ullo; Dustin E. Tillman; Hamza Coban; Katherine G. Stratton; Devin D. Baynes; Alfredo Alexander-Katz; Lindsay B. Case
abstract: Receptor phase separation is common in signaling pathways, yet mechanisms that limit condensate size and drive their dissolution remain poorly understood. For example, phosphorylated EGFR forms large micron-scale condensates in vitro , but assembles into smaller nanoscale clusters in cells, suggesting cellular regulation of condensate size. Here, we show that the intrinsically disordered adaptor protein GAB1 actively dissolves EGFR condensates and re-nucleates smaller, compositionally distinct assemblies in reconstituted supported lipid bilayers and simulations. Dissolution requires unphosphorylated tyrosines within the GAB1 intrinsically disordered region, and tyrosine phosphorylation acts as a regulatory switch that abolishes this activity. GAB1-nucleated assemblies require PH domain-driven oligomerization, which is inhibited by phosphoinositide lipids, linking membrane composition to nucleation. These results uncover two unexpected regulatory features in signaling pathways. First, unphosphorylated tyrosines may function broadly to regulate condensate size or stability, since similar tyrosine-based sequence features are found across hundreds of proteins, including many that function in signal transduction. Additionally, PH domains may play a broader role in protein oligomerization and receptor organization, as an AlphaFold screen reveals dozens of additional PH domains predicted to self-associate. Together, these results establish general mechanisms that function as modular tools for reprogramming signaling through receptor reorganization and may enable new approaches to target such pathways in disease.

title: So similar, yet so different: α-synuclein recognition of the isoform-specific VDAC protein–lipid interface
authors: Rostovtseva TK; Rajendran M; Rosencrans WM; Queralt-Martín M; Wolfe MS; Bautista NA; Beyene BG; Larimi MG; Sodt AJ; Bezrukov SM
abstract:
1. In mammals, VDAC exists as three isoforms – VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 – each characterized by a distinct tissue-dependent distribution and physiologic role. Isoform-specific knockout studies in cells and mice demonstrate distinct physiological roles for each VDAC isoform. The isoforms share about 70% sequence homology and a conserved β-barrel structure and, when reconstituted into planar lipid membranes, form similar highly conductive, anion-selective, voltage-gated channels. A natural question, then, is how relatively minor differences in isoform sequences lead to striking differences in their interactions with protein partners and, consequently, in their physiological functions. To address this question, we used a small, intrinsically disordered cytosolic protein α-synuclein (αSyn) as a sensitive molecular probe. A comparative study with recombinant VDACs reconstituted into planar lipid membranes shows that, depending on the isoform, the αSyn-induced blockage exhibits up to 100-fold differences in on-rates and equilibrium constants. The isoforms also display distinct translocation regimes for αSyn, as evidenced by altered dependences of the off-rates on the applied voltage. Deletion of cysteine residues has a significant effect on αSyn binding. Combined with corresponding data obtained for VDAC2 substates – which show an order of magnitude variation in on-rates while maintaining the conserved equilibrium constants – and the results of molecular dynamics simulations, these findings point to a previously unrecognized step in VDAC inhibition by αSyn: an isoform-specific αSyn interaction with the VDAC protein-lipid interface. This finding opens a new paradigm for understanding VDAC isoform functions and developing isoform-specific therapeutics.

New & Noteworthy

Comparative analysis of α-synuclein interaction with three mammalian VDAC isoforms, complemented by corresponding data for VDAC2 substates and results from molecular dynamics simulations, reveals a new step in the chain of events leading to VDAC blockage. Specifically, our findings point to the isoform-specific interaction of αSyn with VDAC protein-lipid interface, thereby guiding a new strategy in the search for VDAC-targeting drugs.

title: Design of synthetic activators for programmable gene expression
authors: Chen W; Jiao R; Coventry B; Qu X; Bauer M; Tran L; Tcheau T; Wu K; Song Z; Roullier N; Li X; Glasscock C; Hilton IB; Baker D
abstract: Transcription factors control gene expression by recruiting transcriptional coactivators through intrinsically disordered transcriptional activation domains (TADs), whose weak and promiscuous interactions make it difficult to establish quantitative relationships between coactivator recruitment and transcriptional output, and to precisely modulate gene expression. To overcome this limitation, we set out to design coactivator-recruiting proteins using AlphaFold3-predicted TAD-coactivator interactions as a guide. We developed a high-throughput functional screening platform in mammalian cells and identified over 300 well folded nanomolar affinity binders to the transcription coactivators Mediator (multiple subunits), BRD4, NCOA, and p300; targeted interface mutations enabled systematic tuning of their binding affinities. Using a panel of p300 binders spanning nanomolar to micromolar affinities, we found an ultrasensitive relationship between coactivator-binding affinity and transcriptional output, with a sharp transcriptional activation threshold at ∼500 nM. Incorporating p300 binder designs into CRISPRa yielded compact synthetic effectors that drove stronger activation than VPR across multiple genomic loci with minimal detectable cytotoxicity. Combining p300- and Mediator-specific binders further enhanced transcription, revealing functional synergy between these coactivators. Together, our work establishes a quantitative framework linking coactivator-binding affinity to transcriptional output and provides compact synthetic effectors for programmable gene activation.

title: Emergent Entropic Forces Drive Inverse and Reentrant Phase Transitions in Condensates of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
authors: David A. Herrera-Martí; Marc Jamin
abstract: We present a phenomenological, mean-field model for condensates of intrinsically disordered proteins that describes inverse phase transitions and qualitatively predicts reentrant phase behavior as a function of salt concentration. The model is based on a matrix-based formulation of the Flory-Huggins free energy, in which the enthalpic interaction parameter and the protein valence, defined here as the number of effective "sticky patches", are treated as free parameters. Its central insight is that integrating out dynamics of fast-moving molecular species generates an effective entropic force that increases the free-energy barrier to mixing, even within a mean-field description. We account for this by linking Gaussian integration of co-solutes to the Schur complement of the matrix-based Flory-Huggins free energy. This provides a general thermodynamic framework illustrating how enthalpic interactions that increase the number of available microstates necessarily induce effective entropic forces. We demonstrate the expressiveness and predictive power of the model by qualitatively reproducing recent experimental observations on the rabies virus phosphoprotein.
